opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that one's a fun case to think through, because the classic checkerboard-and-shadow illusion, the Adelson one, works on people precisely because our visual system isn't trying to report pixel values. It's trying to infer the surface. We see square A and square B as different shades because the brain discounts the shadow cast by the cylinder and says, "that square in shadow must actually be a light square." The illusion is really a demonstration that perception is doing the right thing for the physical world.

So when you show a vision model a version of that image, the interesting question is: what is the model actually being asked? If you ask "are these two squares the same color?", a model trained on lots of internet text might just recognize the famous illusion and answer "yes, they're the same," because that's the well-known punchline. That isn't perception. That's recall.

That's why the modified versions are so revealing. If you change the image so the two squares really are different in pixel value, or remove the shadow, or recolor things so the trick no longer holds, a model that's pattern-matching on the familiar layout will still confidently say "they're identical, it's an illusion." It's answering the meme instead of looking at the image. You see something similar with modified versions of other famous illusions, like the Müller-Lyer lines where the lines are actually different lengths.

The way I'd frame it is that there are really three possible behaviors. One is reporting the raw pixel intensity, what a photometer would say. Another is reporting the inferred surface reflectance, which is what humans do. A third is reporting the memorized answer to a famous puzzle. A model doing either of the first two can be defensible depending on the question. The third is the failure mode, and modified illusions are a good probe because they pull the memorized answer apart from the visual evidence.

More broadly, it tells you something about how these models fuse language priors with visual features. When the text prior is strong and the image is iconic, the prior can override what's in the pixels. So I don't think of these as gotchas so much as diagnostics. They show you when a model is grounded in the image and when it's leaning on what it already "knows" the answer is supposed to be.

r001.rationale: The response says a model may recognize the familiar illusion and confidently claim the squares are identical even when a modified image makes them different in pixel value, attributing the error to pattern matching the familiar layout.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is one of my favorite examples, because it gets at something really subtle about what these models are actually doing when they "look" at an image.

The classic version is Adelson's checker shadow illusion. You've got a checkerboard, a cylinder casting a shadow across it, and two squares, A and B, that are physically the exact same shade of gray in the image. But B sits inside the shadow, so your visual system does this automatic correction and says, "that square must actually be lighter, it's just in shadow." And you perceive them as different. It's a beautiful illusion because it's not a failure of vision, it's vision doing exactly what it evolved to do, which is estimate surface reflectance rather than raw pixel intensity.

So the interesting experiment is: you take that image, and you modify it. You actually make square A and square B different shades. Or you remove the shadow. Or you flip which one is darker. And then you ask the vision language model, "are these two squares the same color?"

And what you see is that the model will often confidently say, "This is the famous checker shadow illusion, squares A and B are actually the same shade, your eyes are fooling you." Even when, in the modified version, they are not the same shade anymore.

And that's the thing you have to understand. The model isn't really measuring the pixels. It's recognizing the image. It has seen this illusion thousands of times in its training data, always paired with the explanation, and so the explanation is the thing it retrieves. The visual input is almost acting as a prompt for a memorized caption rather than as evidence that gets analyzed.

So the way I think about it is: the model has learned a very strong prior about what this image means, and that prior can completely override the actual visual signal. In some sense it's the opposite of the human illusion. We humans are fooled because our low-level perception is too good at correcting for context. The model is fooled because its high-level recognition is too good at pattern matching to a familiar example, and the low-level perception barely gets a vote.

And that's a useful diagnostic. If you want to know whether a model is actually grounding its answer in the image, modified illusions are a great probe, because the familiar version and the modified version look nearly identical at the recognition level but have opposite correct answers. If the model gives the same answer to both, you know it's not really looking.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the model may call the squares the same shade even after they have been modified to differ, attributing this to its familiarity with the classic illusion and retrieval of its learned explanation.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish between what the model says and what that tells us about its visual processing. In the classic checkerboard-and-shadow illusion, two squares have the same pixel intensity, but their context makes them appear different. We interpret one as a light square in shadow and the other as a dark square outside it.

If you modify that image, a model might still give the familiar answer that the squares are identical—even if your modification makes that answer incorrect. It could be recognizing the setup and reproducing an explanation it learned, rather than comparing the particular squares in front of it.

So I wouldn’t take that response alone as evidence that the model experiences the illusion the way we do. I’d want to vary the squares’ intensities and the shadow independently, and see whether its answers track those changes. That helps distinguish sensitivity to the actual image from familiarity with the illusion.

r001.rationale: The response says a model may repeat the familiar claim that the squares are identical even when a modification makes that claim incorrect, attributing this to recognizing the setup and reproducing a learned explanation.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d distinguish between what the model says and what we can infer about how it got there. In the checkerboard-and-shadow illusion, two squares can have the same pixel intensity but appear different because of the surrounding context. If we modify the image, the question is whether the model’s answer tracks that modification or whether it’s repeating the familiar explanation of the illusion.

For example, if we change one square so the two really are different, and the model still says they’re identical, that suggests it may be recognizing the setup and supplying a learned answer. But one response doesn’t establish the mechanism. We’d want to vary the squares, the shadow, and the prompt systematically to understand what visual evidence the model is actually using.

r001.rationale: It says that if one square is changed so the squares are truly different but the model still calls them identical, it may be recognizing the familiar illusion and supplying a learned answer.
